newsitem.title: KENYA: High interest rates seen hurting Kenyan economy.
newsitem.headline: High interest rates seen hurting Kenyan economy.

text.p: High lending rates are hurting investors and slowing Kenya's economic growth and the situation will not improve in view of prevailing high yields on government securities, bankers and economists said on Friday.

They said the benchmark yield on the 91-day category of government treasury bills was the key reason commercial banks would not lower lending rates, which discouraged local investors and threatened the housing mortages industry.

But the central bank says it has lowered rates on 91-day bills to 21 percent from 24 percent six months ago. Lending rates by commercial banks are in the 25-35 percent range and there is no indication they will decline.
Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) figures showed private sector borrowing rose 14.9 percent between February and February 1996 versus 30.3 percent between April 1995 and April 1996.

The CBK said in its review for April that the outstanding stock of T-bills increased to 95.9 billion shillings ($1.75 billion) in March from 88.1 billion in February due to a rising budget deficit in the first eight months of the fiscal year and inflows of foreign exchange in excess of payments abroad.
Commercial banks hold 62.3 percent of the T-bills stock.
A high risk of non-payment by the private sector in Kenya also meant commercial banks preferred to invest in government securities with guaranteed returns, bankers said.
"As long as the central bank remains in the market competing with commercial banks for deposits, interest rates will not come down," a senior banking consultant said.
"It's very clear that private sector demand for credit from commercial banks has gone down. The high cost of money is putting businessmen off," the consultant added.

Bankers said high lending rates were the result of a vicious chain reaction. To finance a rising budget deficit, the state borrows heavily in the form of treasury bills. To draw investors, the central bank has to offer attractive yields.
"If they reduce the rates, they will no longer be attractive and yet they need to get the money," one banker said.
CBK Chief Banking Manager Reuben Marambii said the real issue remained a stubbornness by commercial banks to adjust lending rates in conform to declining treasury bill yields.
"They're taking everybody for a ride. We do not expect them to offer rates below us, all we're asking them to do is be near us, in both lending and deposit rates," Marambii told Reuters.

But Joseph Kimura, a professor of finance and economist at the private Institute of Policy Analysis and Research said high lending rates by Kenya's commercial banks were indicative of higher inflation rates expected in the future.
Kimura said high lending rates resulted from a complex weave of risks associated with the general economic uncertainty and a possible depreciation of the local currency.
He said a majority of Kenya's 73 banking institutions targetted short-term monetary gain more than social and economic development, which raised rates by 3-5 percentage points.
Commercial bankers said the only solution would be for the CBK to cut rates, possible if government reduced its spending.
Kenya's 1997 GDP growth is now forecast at 4.5 percent, lower than earlier predictions of 7.0 percent.
